n=85: "repeat step two with the fourth and fifth figures and then tell me the count"
c1 imperative repeat complement n1 (step); n2 "two" tied r2; r1 "with" ambiguous c1→n3 ("the fourth and fifth figures": deps the, fourth, and, fifth, head figures); k1 coordination "and" c1, c2; c2 imperative then tell complements n4 (me), n5 (the count).

Hmm: n3 has "and" as a DEPENDENT of "figures" — but "the fourth and fifth figures" — the "and" joins "fourth" and "fifth" (two modifiers). Per the case: a conjunction between two modifier words of one clause may be discourse ("the schema has no wire"). Here "and" is a dependent of the nominal "figures" — hmm, is that acceptable? The case says the conjunction between two modifiers "may be a `discourse` word" and the schema has no wire. Held as a dependent of the nominal — the rule "A word with content is held in discourse" → L2 is the opposite. Here "and" held as a dependent: "Words stand in the wrong wire" (L3)? Hmm.

Hmm. The case explicitly permits discourse for a conjunction between modifiers. Here it's a dependent, which is a different handling; is it wrong? "and" is a linking word (conjunction). Held as a dependent of a nominal — L3 "A linking word is held as a modifier or a dependent"? Is "and" a "linking word"? The marker definition: "`marker` is the linking word: a preposition, `'s`, `if`, the `to` of an infinitive". Conjunctions are "conjunction" of coordinations. So "and" is a conjunction; holding it as a dependent isn't in the L3 list explicitly ("A coordination has a wrong conjunct" is). Hmm.

The case's tolerance for "flat and dry" (discourse) suggests the author is lenient about such conjunctions. But "as a dependent of the nominal" — there's another wrinkle: r1 "with" ends at n3 which contains "and".

I'd accept L8. Hmm, risky but fine. Actually, hmm: is there any lost info? "the fourth and fifth figures" — both held as deps of "figures", "and" as dep too. A next layer can read it. Accept.

n=86: "add a chart with type radar and title Quarterly plan and labels North, South and East and values 3, 5 and 8 and source calendar"
c1 imperative add complement n1; r1 "with" n1→k1 (coordination: n2 type radar, n3 title); k2 coordination "and" n4 (Quarterly plan), n5 (labels) — hmm, k2 joins "Quarterly plan" with "labels"?? That's wrong: "and" joins "title Quarterly plan" with "labels...". Hmm, k2 conjunct n4 (a nominal "Quarterly plan") and n5 ("labels"). And r2 n3→k2 (title → [Quarterly plan and labels]).

Hmm, so "title Quarterly plan and labels" = title with two values? Then k3 joins North, South, East; r3 n5 (labels)→k3. Then k4: coordination with conjunctions and, and; conjuncts c1, c2. c2 fragment complement k6 (coordination n9 values, n13 source calendar) with ellipsis c1. k5 joins 3,5,8; r4 n9→k5.

Words check: add, a, chart, with, type, radar, and, title, Quarterly, plan, and, labels, North, South, and, East, and, values, 3, 5, and, 8, and, source, calendar. That's 6 "and"s? Let me count in text: "type radar and title" (1), "Quarterly plan and labels" (2), "North, South and East" (3), "East and values" (4), "3, 5 and 8" (5), "8 and source" (6). Yes 6.

Circuit "and" count: k1 (1), k2 (1), k3 (1), k4 (2), k5 (1) = 6. OK.

Now the structure: the "with" list should be: type radar, title Quarterly plan, labels North/South/East, values 3/5/8, source calendar. The circuit: k1 = [type radar, title] with r2 title→k2=[Quarterly plan, labels], r3 labels→k3=[North,South,East], and then a separate fragment c2 with complement k6=[values, source calendar] with ellipsis c1, joined to c1 by k4 (with 2 "and"s).

Hmm, so "type radar and title" as one coordination: "a chart with type radar and title" — k1 joins the two properties correctly (type radar, title). Then "title [Quarterly plan and labels]" — r2 from n3 (title) to k2 (Quarterly plan, labels): so "title" is linked to its value "Quarterly plan" and also to "labels"?! That makes "labels" a value of the title. Then "labels" → k3 (the three label names). Hmm — "Quarterly plan and labels" merged as the title's values: the title value should be "Quarterly plan" only, and "labels" is the next property name. k2 joining "Quarterly plan" with "labels" as one coordination under "title" is a wrong coordination: the "and" joins "title Quarterly plan" with "labels North, South and East" (both list items of "with"), not "Quarterly plan" with "labels".

Rule L3: "A coordination has a wrong conjunct." Here k2's conjuncts are "Quarterly plan" and "labels" — the message's "and" joins the title property with the labels property. Hmm, but joining the values is a chain reading: "title [Quarterly plan] and [labels...]" — the coordination joins the value with the next property name, which differs from joining the properties (n3 title with n5 labels).

Compare the k4 handling: c1/c2 coordination covered "and values..." So the formalizer is inconsistent: some "and"s join values to next property names, some join clauses.

Given the "with"-list pattern in n=30 (which I accepted), here the structure seems muddled but each word is placed and tied. Is there a *specific wrong statement*? "labels" being a conjunct with "Quarterly plan" under "title" says the title has two values "Quarterly plan" and "labels..." — that's wrong-ish but the "chain" reading is loose.

Hmm. This is the kind of case where I need to decide: the message is a long property list; the formalizer's chain of relations is plausible-ish. The rules demand: is there a wrong statement? The coordination k2 joining "Quarterly plan" with "labels" — I'd say grammar-wise, "title Quarterly plan and labels North, South and East" the "and" joins the property "title Quarterly plan" with the property "labels ...", or "Quarterly plan" with "labels"? Ambiguous! Since this is a list without commas ("title Quarterly plan and labels North, South and East and values 3, 5 and 8 and source calendar"), repeated "and"s. Hmm, plausible. Accept L8.

Hmm, hold on. n=30 was similar and I accepted. For consistency, accept n=86.

n=87: "change a meteing Main Track 3 1 Review"
n1 = "change a meteing 3 1 Review" (deps change, a, meteing, 3, 1, head Review); n2 "Main Track" (dep Main, head Track); c1 fragment complements n1, n2.

"change" is the verb (command) — held as a dependent of "Review" → the command is lost → L5 (verb held as a dependent, no clause has it) or L1 (command needs its verb; "change" is a verb). "change" could be a noun ("a change"), so the settled L1 case applies: "When the first word of a message with no other verb can be a noun or a verb ('book design review', 'schedule the kickoff'), it is the verb; held as a noun in a fragment, the command is lost: L1."

Here "change" is the first word; the message is garbled ("a meteing Main Track 3 1 Review" — probably "change a meeting Main Track 3 1 Review"). Held as a dependent → command lost → L1. Yes, L1 (per the settled case, which explicitly says L1).

Quote 'change a'. Note: "'change' is the first word and the only verb, but it is held as a dependent of 'Review', so the command is lost."

L1.

n=88: "right, for the board meeting make a pie chart of the results, Chat uh 5; Phone 5, Email 85"
c1 imperative discourse right, verb make, complement n2 (a pie chart); r1 "for" c1→n1; r2 "of" n2→n3 (the results); n4 Chat; c2 fragment discourse uh complement n4; n5 5; n6 Phone; n7 5; n8 Email; n9 85; k1 coordination conjunct c1, c2, c3; r3 n4→n5; c3 fragment complement n6; r4 n6→n7; r5 n6→n8; r6 n8→n9.

Hmm. "Chat uh 5" — "uh" as discourse of the fragment c2 — fine (garbled filler). Values: Chat 5, Phone 5, Email 85. The circuit ties n4→n5 (Chat 5), n6→n7 (Phone 5), n6→n8 (Phone → Email! wrong), n8→n9 (Email 85). r5 n6→n8 ties "Phone" to "Email", which is a spurious relation... but every item must be tied to something. Hmm, c3 fragment complement n6 (Phone) with r5 to Email — this is a chain: Phone tied to Email. Hmm.

Is r5 wrong? It asserts a tie between Phone and Email that the message doesn't give (they're separate list items separated by a semicolon/comma). L4: "a relation ... between wires that the message does not relate". Hmm, but a chain tie is how the formalizer keeps them from being untied. The alternative: c3's complement could be k (coordination) of Phone and Email rather than a relation...

Hmm. The pairing "Phone 5" and "Email 85" are given; here "Phone" is tied to "5" (r4) and to "Email" (r5), and "Email" to "85" (r6). So the pairs are right; the extra tie n6→n8 links the two items. Is that "a relation between wires that the message does not relate"? List items are related by juxtaposition; the tie is a chain. A next layer reads: results: Chat 5, Phone 5, Email 85, with Phone→Email tie. Slightly odd but recoverable.

Hmm, L4 vs L8. Given the "coordination" chain reading (like n=86 which I accepted), accept L8.

n=89: "Somewhere on that slide there should be a bar chart titled Intro, labels Main, values Second"
c1 declarative modifier Somewhere, auxiliary should, verb be, subject n2 (there), complement n3 (a bar chart); r1 "on" c1→n1 (that slide); c2 nonfinite titled complement n4 (Intro); n5 labels; n6 Main; n7 values; n8 Second; r2 n3→c2; r3 n3→n5; r4 n3→n7; r5 n5→n6; r6 n7→n8.

Good: labels/value pairs tied from the property names, and the property names tied to the chart. Acceptable. L8.

n=90: "the man in the orange jacket and blue hat to the right end, and then the boy in the purple jacket and red hat between the middle and the right end"
n1 the man; r1 "in" n1→k1 (orange jacket, blue hat); r2 "to" n1→n4 (the right end); k2 coordination "and" n1, n5 (the boy); n5 = "then the boy" (deps then, the, head boy); r3 "in" n5→k3 (purple jacket, red hat); r4 "between" n5→k4 (the middle, the right end); c1 fragment complement k2.

Hmm: "then" held as a DEPENDENT of "boy"! n5 deps: "then", "the", head "boy". Per the settled case: "A word of time or order cannot describe a noun from where it stands ... it is a `modifier` of the clause; held as a `dependent`, it fails: L3."

"then" as a dependent of "boy" → L3. Quote 'then the boy' — hmm, careful: the quote must be words of the message: "then the boy" — the message has "and then the boy in the purple". Yes "then the boy" appears in the message ("... and then the boy in the purple jacket"). Good.

So n=90 → L3.

n=91: "rotate upside dwn"
n1 "rotate"; n2 "upside"; c1 imperative verb "dwn" complement n2; c2 fragment complement n1; k1 coordination c2, c1.

"dwn" is misspelt "down"; held as the verb of an imperative with complement "upside". And "rotate" held as a nominal in a fragment. Hmm — "rotate" is the verb (command): "rotate upside down". Held as a nominal "rotate" in a fragment → the command is lost → L1 per the settled case ("When the first word of a message with no other verb can be a noun or a verb ... it is the verb; held as a noun in a fragment, the command is lost: L1"). "rotate" is basically only a verb. So L1.

Quote 'rotate upside'.

n=92: "I changed my mind: the diagram I have open."
c1 declarative changed subject I complement my mind; n3 the diagram; n4 I; c2 declarative have subject n4 (no complement — "open"?); c3 fragment modifier "open" complement n3; k1 coordination c1, c3; r1 n3→c2.

Hmm: "the diagram I have open" — relative clause "I have open". c2 = "I have" (verb have, subject I), c3 fragment modifier open with complement the diagram. The "open" as modifier of c3... and c3 coordinated with c1. Hmm.

The words: I, changed, my, mind, the, diagram, I, have, open. Placed: n1 I, c1 changed + my mind, n3 the diagram, n4 I, c2 have, c3 modifier open complement n3, k1 c1&c3, r1 n3→c2.

Is the structure acceptable? "the diagram I have open" = "the diagram [that] I have open" — the relative clause "I have open" is c2 + "open" (a complement/adjective). The circuit splits "open" into a separate fragment clause c3 (complement the diagram) coordinated with c1. Hmm, that's odd but the words are placed and tied: c2 (I have) tied from n3; "open" (c3) tied? c3 is coordinated with c1 via k1 — so "open" is tied to c1 (I changed my mind). Hmm.

The message: "I changed my mind: the diagram I have open." — the second part is "the diagram I have open" (a fragment naming the intended target). The circuit's c3 = fragment with modifier "open" and complement "the diagram"; coordinated with c1 (I changed my mind) — that's a coordination joining the declarative c1 with the fragment c3. Loose but okay?

Hmm, "open" as a modifier of c3 rather than part of the relative clause "I have open" (as its complement) — c2 "I have" has no complement, and "open" is in c3. So the relative clause "I have open" is broken: the adjective "open" is separated. Is that a wrong statement? c2: "I have" with no complement — the thing been had is "the diagram" (tied via r1 n3→c2). So "the diagram [which] I have" + "open" separately. The reading "the diagram I have open" is roughly recoverable: "open" describes the diagram (c3 complement n3) which is close to right.

Hmm. Modifier vs complement — "what a modifier says" not judged. I'd accept L8.

n=93: "here is the plan: the inheritance arrows hollow, plus mark the parent class at the arrow tail, so it still fits on a single slide without crowding"
c1 declarative modifier here verb is subject n1 (the plan); n2 the inheritance arrows; c2 declarative verb "hollow" subject n2!! — "the inheritance arrows hollow" — "hollow" is an adjective; held as the verb of a declarative clause → L1? ("Its verb is a word that is no verb here"). Hmm, per the settled case: "A message or a part with no verb ('pie radius smaller', 'legend on the right', 'a fireplace') is a fragment. Its nominals that are not the end of a relation are its complement. A noun made its verb is L1."

Here "hollow" (an adjective) is made the verb of a declarative clause → same family: L1. The correct handling: c2 should be a fragment with "hollow" as modifier.

Hmm, but wait: is "hollow" possibly a verb ("hollow out")? "the inheritance arrows hollow" — no, adjective. So L1: "Its verb is a word that is no verb here".

Hmm, or is this L3 (head wrong)? L1 is first. Quote 'the inheritance arrows hollow'.

Hmm, also "plus mark..." k1 joins c1, c2, c3 with "plus" — hmm, "plus" twice? Text has "plus" once. k1 conjunction="plus" once for 3 conjuncts. OK.

n=94: "I want the long bench a bit closer to the path, and leave the path clear."
c1 declarative want modifier closer subject I complements n2 (the long bench), n3 (a bit); r1 "to" c1→n4 (the path); k1 coordination "and" c1, c2; c2 declarative verb leave modifier clear complement n5 (the path).

Hmm, c2 "leave the path clear" — written as declarative with verb "leave"! It's a command ("leave the path clear"). Per the settled case for verbs after "and": "a verb after 'and' ... that follows a clause with a subject and an auxiliary, in the form that auxiliary takes, may share them: a clause with no subject of its own, declarative or nonfinite. Written as a command, imperative, it passes too."

Hmm — but does this apply only when the first clause has a subject AND an auxiliary? Here c1 "I want" has a subject "I" but no auxiliary. The case: "'the Gate box should go right under Path, and align their tops' ... a verb after 'and' or 'then' that follows a clause with a `subject` and an `auxiliary`, in the form that auxiliary takes, may share them". Here there's no auxiliary, so "leave" as declarative doesn't share an auxiliary-based form. Hmm, but sharing the subject "I"? "I want ..., and leave the path clear" — hmm, as declarative "I leave" would need the subject written.

So c2 as declarative with verb "leave" and no subject: states "leave the path clear" — as a declarative parse, the subject would be shared from "I"? Hmm, the case requires an auxiliary in the first clause to allow this. Without it, "and leave the path clear" is a command → written declarative is a wrong form → L1.

Hmm, but is it "a clear question written as imperative or declarative, or the reverse"? L1 covers questions and fragments. For a command written as declarative, the settled "Have the legend switched on" case says interrogative fails L1 — the reverse.

Hmm, but the other settled case (verbs after "and") explicitly allows declarative sharing of subject/auxiliary. Here there is a subject "I" but no auxiliary. Is "leave" sharing "I"? "I want ... and leave the path clear" — grammatically, "I want X and leave Y" is a valid coordination "I [want X] and [leave Y]". Hmm! Actually yes: "I want the long bench a bit closer to the path, and leave the path clear" reads as an imperative? Hmm, in a diagram-tool context, "I want ... and leave the path clear" — the intent is a command "leave the path clear".

Grammatically, "I want ..., and leave the path clear" — a declarative reading works if the subject "I" is shared. The circuit's c2 has no subject of its own → sharing "I". This matches the settled allowance (a clause with no subject of its own, declarative) except the auxiliary condition.

Hmm, the case says "follows a clause with a `subject` and an `auxiliary`" — that's the "should go ... and align" example. Here only a subject. I'd be lenient: c1 has a subject, so c2 with no subject sharing "I" is a plausible reading. Hmm, but then "leave the path clear" is a command and the "I" sharing is wrong (the user isn't saying "I leave").

Hmm. Which is more likely the reference judgment? I think the formalizer chose declarative because it's the same pattern as the settled case. Given the message is "I want the long bench a bit closer to the path, and leave the path clear." — the second part is an imperative.

Note also: "a bit closer" — "closer" as modifier of c1, "a bit" as a complement (measure) — allowed.

Hmm, is c2's declarative form a rejection? L1's form criterion is about questions and verbs-as-fragments. It does not list "a command written as declarative". Hmm! Let me re-read L1: "A clause that the circuit writes is wrong. Its `form` is wrong: a clear question written as `imperative` or `declarative`, or the reverse; a clause with a verb written as `fragment`."

So form errors listed: (a) clear question ↔ imperative/declarative; (b) clause with verb written as fragment. A command written as declarative is not listed. So no L1.

Is there another grade? L3? "Words stand in the wrong wire"? Not really. So arguably acceptable. The next layer can read "I want X and leave Y" and interpret as a command. I'll accept L8.

Hmm, but hold on: does c2 lack something? c2 verb leave, modifier clear, complement the path. Grammar fine.

Accept n=94.

n=95: "right, for readers who skim I'd like the first paragraph moved before the chapter heading, with the remaining blocks in order"
c1 declarative discourse right, auxiliary 'd, verb like, subject n2 (I); r1 "for" c1→n1 (readers); r2 "who" n1→c2 (declarative skim); n3 the first paragraph; c3 nonfinite moved subject n3; r3 "before" c3→n4; r4 "with" c3→c4 (fragment complement n5 the remaining blocks); r5 "in" n5→n6 (order); r6 c1→c3; c4 fragment complement n5.

"titled"? no. Looks fine: c3 nonfinite "moved" with subject n3, tied to c1. r4 "with" from c3 to c4 — "with the remaining blocks in order" attached to "moved" — plausible.

Accept L8.

n=96: "create a timeline of the hiring rounds, left to right, with even gaps between the ticks"
c1 imperative create complement n1 (a timeline); r1 "of" n1→n2 (the hiring rounds); n3 "left"; r2 "to" n3→n4 ("right"); r3 "with" ambiguous c1→n5 (even gaps); r4 "between" n5→n6 (the ticks); r5 n1→n3.

"left to right" — n3 "left" and n4 "right" as nominals with r2 "to" between them. Acceptable ("left to right" — a distance/manner phrase). Hmm, could be modifiers. Fine.

Accept L8.

Continue with 97-108.

n=97: "a little bird up in the top right, then place the green block one space left and a quarter space up but never touching the blue block, no other change, so the spacing comes out even"
c1 fragment modifier up complement n1 (a little bird); r1 "in" c1→n2 ("the top right": deps the, top, head right); k1 coordination with conjunctions then, and, but, so and conjuncts c1, c2, c5, c4; c2 imperative place modifier left, up, complements n3 (green block), n4 (one space), n5 (a quarter space); c3 nonfinite "never touching" complement n6; n7 "no other change"; n8 the spacing; c4 declarative "comes" modifier out, modifier even, subject n8; r2 c2→c3; c5 fragment complement n7.

Words: a little bird, up, in, the top right, then, place, the green block, one space, left, and, a quarter space, up, but, never, touching, the blue block, no other change, so, the spacing, comes, out, even.

Circuit count "up": c1 modifier "up", c2 modifier "up" — two ups; text has "a little bird up in" (1) and "a quarter space up" (2). Good. "and": k1 conjunction "and" (1) — text "one space left and a quarter space up" (1). Good. "but": k1 (1). "so": k1 (1). "then": k1 (1) — text "then place" (1).

Structure: c2's complements: n3 (green block), n4 (one space), n5 (a quarter space); modifiers left, up. Hmm — "one space left" and "a quarter space up": two measures; "left" and "up" as modifiers of c2. Per the "n=5" pattern ("three spaces left") acceptable: measures as nominals, directions as modifiers. Here two measures and two directions in one clause — the pairing again lost (like n=44). Hmm.

That's the same pattern as n=44, which I was leaning to reject. Consistency matters. In n=44: "the red block one place left and the blue block one place right" — two things, two measures, two directions, all in one fragment.

Here n=97: "place the green block one space left and a quarter space up" — one thing, two measures ("one space left", "a quarter space up"), two directions merged as modifiers of c2. A next layer recovers "place the green block, one space, a quarter space, left, up" — the pairing of left↔one space is lost-ish but the order is preserved (measure1, left, measure2, up). Hmm, since modifiers and complements are unordered lists, the pairing is lost. Is that a "wrong statement"? Hmm. It says the block goes both left and up by both distances — a compound move which is actually what's meant ("one space left and a quarter space up" = diagonal move: left 1 and up 0.25). So actually merging is semantically OK! The move is both left and up. In n=44, the two things are different blocks (red left, blue right) — there merging applies both directions to both blocks — that IS wrong (red shouldn't go right).

So n=97 accept L8 (a single diagonal move), while n=44 reject (two different objects).

Let me double check n=44 again: "the red block one place left and the blue block one place right" — the circuit: c1 fragment with modifiers left, right; complements k2 (red block, blue block), n2, n4 (one place each). So both directions apply to the same pair → the red block goes right? No: modifiers are on the clause whose complements are both blocks. That's a wrong statement for the red block (it goes left, not right). So L3 or L6. I'll keep rejecting n=44. Grade: I said L3 initially, then L6. Let me think again: "A pairing the words give is not written" — L6 is about a word tied to nothing. Here the information "which block goes left" is lost. Hmm, L3: "Words stand in the wrong wire" — the words 'right' and 'one place' of the blue block's instruction stand in the clause of the red block's instruction. That fits L3: words of one written clause in another... which is L1's phrasing.

Hmm! L1: "Words of one written clause are held in another." The first part is one written part "the red block one place left" and the second "the blue block one place right". Two parts; the circuit writes one clause c1 holding words from both. So the second part's words ('right', 'one place') are held in the first party clause → L1.

Hmm, but are these "written clauses"? They have no verbs → fragments. c1 is a fragment clause; the second part's fragment clause is not written at all.

Ugh. I'll go with L3 (words in the wrong wire): the note can be: "'right' and the second 'one place' stand in the same fragment as 'left', so the red block is said to move right as well" — names the wrong statement.

Hmm, actually a cleaner L3 framing: "a tie is wrong" — r? The directions are modifiers, not relations. OK, L3.

n=98: "a bench goes in the middle of the scene, and a tree set on every side of it"
c1 declarative goes subject n1 (a bench); r1 "in" c1→n2; r2 "of" n2→n3; k1 coordination "and" c1, c2; n4 a tree; c2 nonfinite "set" subject n4; r3 "on" c2→n5 (every side); r4 "of" n5→n6 (it).

Acceptable? c2 nonfinite "set" with subject n4 ("a tree set on every side of it"). Fine. Accept L8.

n=99: "How about a column chart of claims by region for 2024 and then a parallel chart for 2023 on a shared y axis and then give the first chart the title 'Claims by region, two years'"
c1 fragment modifier "How"; r1 "about" c1→k2 (coordination n1 a column chart, n5 "then a parallel chart"); r2 "of" n1→n2 (claims); r3 "by" n2→n3 (region); r4 "for" n1→n4 (2024); k1 coordination with conjunctions and, and; conjuncts c1, c2; n5 "then a parallel chart" — "then" as a DEPENDENT of "chart"! → L3 per the settled case (word of order held as dependent of a nominal).

Hmm: n5 syntax.nominal dependent="then" dependent="a" dependent="parallel" head="chart". "then" as a dependent of "chart" → the thing becomes "the then parallel chart". Per the settled case: "A word of time or order cannot describe a noun from where it stands ... held as a dependent, it fails: L3."

Also c2 has modifier "then" too (c2 modifiers: then). Text has "then" twice ("and then a parallel chart", "and then give the first chart") — so one "then" in n5 as dependent, one as c2's modifier. The one in n5 is misplaced.

So n=99 → L3, quoting 'then a parallel chart'.

n=100: "make the avatar a guy, human"
c1 imperative make complements n1 (the avatar), n2 (a guy); n3 "human"; r1 n2→n3.

Fine. "human" tied to "a guy". Accept L8.

n=101: "just undo the latest, whatever it was"
c1 imperative modifier just, verb undo, complement n1 (the latest); r1 "whatever" n1→c2 (declarative was subject it). Fine. "whatever it was" — a clause tied to "the latest". Marker "whatever" — hmm, is "whatever" a linking word? It's a relative word; using it as a marker is plausible. Accept L8.

n=102: "could you place a tree twice as tall as the boy — the way the drawing looks so far — exactly where the picture needs it"
c1 interrogative could place modifiers twice, as, tall, exactly, subject you, complement n2 (a tree); r1 "as" c1→n3 (the boy); n4 "the way"; n5 the drawing; c2 declarative looks, modifier so, modifier far, subject n5; r2 "where" c1→c3 (needs); r3 n2→n4; r4 n4→c2.

Hmm: "the way the drawing looks so far" — n4 "the way" tied from n2 (tree) and to c2. Fine (as n=20).
